summary.text: A direct finite calculation checks the required property at 43 and, for every \(44\le k\le288\), exhibits an admissible base whose expansion has three distinct digits. For \(k\ge289\), write \(b=\lfloor\sqrt{k}\rfloor\) and \(k=b^2+d\) with \(0\le d\le2b\); a case split on \(d\) selects one of the nearby bases \(b,b-1,b-2,b-3\), where the resulting three-digit expansion has explicitly pairwise-distinct digits.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D_b(n)\) denote the set of distinct digits occurring in the usual base-\(b\) expansion of \(n\). We must prove two assertions:

1. \(|D_b(43)|\le 2\) for every integer \(b\) with \(3\le b<43\);
2. for every \(k>43\), there is some integer \(b\) with \(3\le b<k\) such that \(|D_b(k)|\ge 3\).

Together these say exactly that \(43\) satisfies the defining condition and no larger integer does.

## 1. A three-digit obstruction

We begin with a basic observation about positional expansions. Suppose that \(b\ge2\) and
\[
b^2\le n<b^3.
\]
Repeated Euclidean division by \(b\) shows that the base-\(b\) expansion of \(n\), written from least significant digit to most significant digit, is
\[
\left(n\bmod b,\;\left\lfloor\frac nb\right\rfloor\bmod b,\;\left\lfloor\frac n{b^2}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
Indeed, the first division gives the units digit \(n\bmod b\) and quotient \(\lfloor n/b\rfloor\); dividing that quotient by \(b\) gives the second digit and quotient \(\lfloor n/b^2\rfloor\). The inequality \(n<b^3\) makes the latter quotient less than \(b\), while \(n\ge b^2\) makes it nonzero, so there are exactly three digits.

Consequently, if these three displayed numbers are pairwise distinct, then \(D_b(n)\) has at least three elements. In that case \(n\) cannot satisfy the defining condition, provided also that \(3\le b<n\).

A particularly useful special case is this. If
\[
n=b^2+ub+v,
\]
where \(0\le u,v<b\) and \(n<2b^2\), then the three base-\(b\) digits, from least to most significant, are
\[
(v,u,1).
\]
Thus, whenever \(v,u,1\) are pairwise distinct, base \(b\) is an obstruction.

## 2. The finite checks

### The number \(43\)

For completeness, direct division gives the following sets of digits for \(43\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
b&D_b(43)&b&D_b(43)&b&D_b(43)\\ \hline
3&\{1,2\}&4&\{2,3\}&5&\{1,3\}\\
6&\{1\}&7&\{1,6\}&8&\{3,5\}\\
9&\{4,7\}&10&\{3,4\}&11&\{3,10\}\\
12&\{3,7\}&13&\{3,4\}&14&\{1,3\}\\
15&\{2,13\}&16&\{2,11\}&17&\{2,9\}\\
18&\{2,7\}&19&\{2,5\}&20&\{2,3\}\\
21&\{1,2\}&22&\{1,21\}&23&\{1,20\}\\
24&\{1,19\}&25&\{1,18\}&26&\{1,17\}\\
27&\{1,16\}&28&\{1,15\}&29&\{1,14\}\\
30&\{1,13\}&31&\{1,12\}&32&\{1,11\}\\
33&\{1,10\}&34&\{1,9\}&35&\{1,8\}\\
36&\{1,7\}&37&\{1,6\}&38&\{1,5\}\\
39&\{1,4\}&40&\{1,3\}&41&\{1,2\}\\
42&\{1\}&&&
\end{array}
\]
Every one of these sets has at most two elements. Hence \(43\) satisfies the required condition.

### The interval \(44\le k\le288\)

This finite interval is disposed of by direct base expansion. The following table partitions all the integers from \(44\) through \(288\). An integer \(k\) listed in the row headed by \(b\) has at least three distinct digits in base \(b\). The entries such as \(45\text{--}48\) denote all integers in that interval.

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
b&k\\ \hline
3&45\text{--}48,51,55,57\text{--}59,61,63\text{--}66,69,73,75,83,86\text{--}89,92,\\

&189\text{--}201,204,207\text{--}210,213,217,219\text{--}221,223,225\text{--}228,231,235,\\

\]

Each assertion in the table is obtained by repeated Euclidean division of \(k\) by the indicated base and observing at least three different remainders/digits. Thus every \(k\) in this interval has an admissible base \(b\): all the displayed bases lie between \(3\) and \(9\), hence are certainly less than \(k\). Therefore no \(k\) with \(44\le k\le288\) satisfies the condition.

It remains to treat all \(k\ge289\).

## 3. Parametric obstructions

We record several elementary families. In each line, the indicated number \(n\) has the displayed three digits in the indicated base \(q\), listed from least significant to most significant:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{family}&n&\text{base}&\text{digits}\\ \hline
A&(q+3)^2=q^2+6q+9&q&(9,6,1),\quad q\ge14\\
B&(q+2)^2+1=q^2+4q+5&q&(5,4,1),\quad q\ge6\\
C&(q+2)^2+(q+2)+1=q^2+5q+7&q&(7,5,1),\quad q\ge8\\
D&(q+3)^2+2(q+3)-2=q^2+8q+13&q&(13,8,1),\quad q\ge14\\
E&q^2+e&q&(e,0,1),\quad q\ge17,\ 2\le e<q\\
F&q^2+3q+2&q&(2,3,1),\quad q\ge16\\
G&q^2+3q+2+e&q&(2+e,3,1),\quad q\ge16,\ 2\le e<q-2\\
H&q^2+4q&q&(0,4,1),\quad q\ge16\\
I&q^2+4q+2&q&(2,4,1),\quad q\ge16\\
J&q^2+2q&q&(0,2,1),\quad q\ge17.
\end{array}
\]

Let us justify all the information in this table. In every row the displayed identity is immediate by expansion. The constant terms and linear coefficients are less than \(q\) under the stated lower bounds. In row \(G\), the hypothesis \(e<q-2\) gives \(2+e<q\). Thus the displayed coefficients really are base-\(q\) digits.

They are pairwise distinct. This is immediate in rows \(A,B,C,D,F,H,I,J\). In row \(E\), \(2\le e<q\), so \(e\), \(0\), and \(1\) are distinct. In row \(G\), \(e\ge2\), so \(2+e\ge4\), and hence \(2+e\), \(3\), and \(1\) are distinct.

For clarity, there is no hidden issue involving an additional leading digit. In each row the amount added to \(q^2\) is strictly less than \(q^2\). The only inequalities that are not completely immediate are
\[
6q+9<q^2\quad(q\ge14),\qquad
4q+5<q^2\quad(q\ge6),
\]
\[
5q+7<q^2\quad(q\ge8),\qquad
8q+13<q^2\quad(q\ge14).
\]
Each holds at the stated endpoint and its right side thereafter grows faster; equivalently, subtracting the left side gives respectively positive quadratics. For row \(G\),
\[
3q+2+e<4q<q^2
\]
because \(e<q-2\) and \(q\ge16\). The remaining rows are even more immediate. Hence in all rows
\[
q^2\le n<2q^2<q^3.
\]
The three-digit observation from Section 1 therefore applies and gives exactly the triples in the table.

Finally, every base in the table is admissible: \(q\ge3\), and \(q<n\) because \(n\ge q^2\) and \(q>1\). Thus every number belonging to one of these families fails the defining condition.

## 4. Reduction of every \(k\ge289\) to one of the families

Fix \(k\ge289\), and put
\[
b=\lfloor\sqrt{k}\rfloor,
\qquad
d=k-b^2.
\]
Since \(17^2=289\), we have \(b\ge17\). By the defining property of the integer square root,
\[
b^2\le k<(b+1)^2=b^2+2b+1.
\]
Thus
\[
k=b^2+d,\qquad 0\le d\le2b.
\]
We now exhaust all possible values of \(d\). In each case we rewrite \(k\) in one of the forms above. This sometimes uses a nearby base such as \(b-1\), \(b-2\), or \(b-3\).

### Case 1: \(d=0\)

Set \(q=b-3\). Then \(q\ge14\), and
\[
k=b^2=(q+3)^2.
\]
This is family \(A\), so base \(b-3\) exhibits three distinct digits \(9,6,1\).

### Case 2: \(d=1\)

Set \(q=b-2\). Then \(q\ge15\), in particular \(q\ge6\), and
\[
k=b^2+1=(q+2)^2+1.
\]
This is family \(B\), with digits \(5,4,1\) in base \(b-2\).

### Case 3: \(2\le d<b\)

Here we use base \(b\) itself. We have
\[
k=b^2+d,
\]
so family \(E\) applies with \(q=b\) and \(e=d\). The digits are \(d,0,1\), which are pairwise distinct.

We may now suppose that \(d\ge b\).

### Case 4: \(d=b\)

Set \(q=b-1\). Since \(b\ge17\), \(q\ge16\), and a direct expansion gives
\[
q^2+3q+2=(b-1)^2+3(b-1)+2=b^2+b=k.
\]
Thus family \(F\) applies, giving digits \(2,3,1\) in base \(b-1\).

### Case 5: \(d=b+1\)

Set \(q=b-2\). Then \(q\ge15\), hence \(q\ge8\), and
\[
(q+2)^2+(q+2)+1=b^2+b+1=k.
\]
This is family \(C\), with digits \(7,5,1\) in base \(b-2\).

We may now suppose that \(d\ge b+2\).

### Case 6: \(b+2\le d<2b-2\)

Put
\[
e=d-b.
\]
Then \(e\ge2\), and \(d<2b-2\) gives \(e<b-2\). We split off the upper endpoint that arises because \(e\) is integral.

First suppose \(e<b-3\). Let \(q=b-1\). Then \(q\ge16\), and
\[
e<(b-1)-2=q-2.
\]
Moreover,
\[
q^2+3q+2+e
=(b-1)^2+3(b-1)+2+e
=b^2+b+e
=b^2+d
=k.
\]
Thus family \(G\) applies. Its three digits in base \(b-1\) are \(2+e,3,1\).

The only remaining possibility in the present range is \(e=b-3\): indeed, we know \(e<b-2\) but not \(e<b-3\). In that event \(d=b+e=2b-3\). Again put \(q=b-1\). Then
\[
q^2+4q=(b-1)^2+4(b-1)=b^2+2b-3=k.
\]
This is family \(H\), whose digits in base \(b-1\) are \(0,4,1\).

This exhausts all \(d<2b-2\).

### Case 7: \(d=2b-2\)

Set \(q=b-3\), so \(q\ge14\). Then \(q+3=b\), and
\[
(q+3)^2+2(q+3)-2=b^2+2b-2=k.
\]
Family \(D\) applies, giving digits \(13,8,1\) in base \(b-3\).

### Case 8: \(d=2b-1\)

Set \(q=b-1\), so \(q\ge16\). Expanding,
\[
q^2+4q+2=(b-1)^2+4(b-1)+2=b^2+2b-1=k.
\]
This is family \(I\), with digits \(2,4,1\) in base \(b-1\).

### Case 9: \(d=2b\)

Use base \(b\). We have
\[
k=b^2+2b,
\]
which is family \(J\), with digits \(0,2,1\).

These cases are exhaustive because \(0\le d\le2b\): we treated \(d=0\), \(d=1\), the interval \(2\le d<b\), then \(d=b\), \(d=b+1\), the interval \(b+2\le d<2b-2\), and finally the three values \(2b-2,2b-1,2b\).

In every case we have produced a base at least \(3\) and less than \(k\) in which \(k\) has at least three distinct digits. Therefore no \(k\ge289\) satisfies the defining condition.

Combining this general argument with the finite check for \(44\le k\le288\), every integer larger than \(43\) fails the condition. Since the earlier table proves that \(43\) itself satisfies it, the sequence is finite and its last term is \(43\), as claimed.
